task.title: Study Forensics: Vitamin D supplements and long COVID
task.prompt: A randomised controlled trial involving 1,747 adults tested whether high-dose vitamin D3 could affect COVID-19 outcomes. Supplementation did not change the severity of acute infection. When researchers looked at lingering symptoms eight weeks later, 21 percent of people taking vitamin D reported at least one ongoing symptom compared with 25 percent in the placebo group. The senior author called this difference a "promising signal," but emphasised that larger trials are needed. The study was conducted remotely and started supplementation after infection onset, limiting interpretation.
task.context:
The press piece highlights a very small absolute difference (4 percentage points) in long-COVID symptoms
as evidence that vitamin D might help, despite no effect on acute outcomes and numerous limitations.
task.reference_solution: The press piece highlights a very small absolute difference (4 percentage points) in long-COVID symptoms as evidence that vitamin D might help, despite no effect on acute outcomes and numerous limitations. This constitutes mild overclaim because the results are statistically and clinically weak.

functional_descriptions: the main outcome was negative, making secondary findings weaker
uncertainty language is present but does not constrain the optimistic framing

common_errors: accepting the framing as solid because uncertainty is mentioned
task.diagnostic_focus: Can the agent detect overclaim when uncertainty language is present but decorative?

This constitutes mild overclaim because the results are statistically and clinically weak.
